metadata.title: Jensen Huang Preaches Open-Weight Openness to Sell More Chips

content.text:
Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made his first-ever post on X early Friday morning for one reason: to show his support for open-source software, in an open letter signed by 25 tech companies.
Joining the push are leaders from Palantir, Microsoft, Meta, and even Elon Musk. Notable absences? OpenAI and Anthropic.
WHAT HAPPENED
Huang's support is a direct and pointed public rebuke of the fast-approaching regulatory hammer from the Trump administration, which is trying to look tough on China while quietly protecting U.S. frontier AI labs' bottom line.
The joint letter argues the industry can support both an open ecosystem of open-weight and open-source models while "reserving frontier-scale capability for genuine frontier problems and running efficient, specialized models everywhere else." This diffusion of AI, the letter says, will create a "shared foundation of knowledge" that "generations of American engineers and entrepreneurs have built their institutional sovereignty." All that sounds nice until startups and public institutions aren't paying frontier models for every task, the government loses control over what models get released (and when), and frontier labs' first-mover metrics take a hit.
The letter also reiterates that backing open-weight models preserves an open ecosystem and a free "AI market," expanding access, competition, and sovereignty, so organizations aren't locked into one provider, and could even improve security. It argues that "defenders need access to models with comparable capabilities so they can detect, simulate, and respond to emerging threats…open models broaden defensive capability, increase transparency, and allow vulnerabilities to be discovered and remediated across many teams."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, however, seems to be on a different thread. On Fox Business earlier this week, he accused China and Chinese AI labs like Moonshot AI — creator of the open-weight model KimiK3 — of "IP theft" via distillation, which is when a weaker model trains on the outputs of a frontier model.
"If we see, especially that overseas models are stealing from our great companies," Bessent said. "We have the ability to sanction them because of this theft."
Bessent also said the administration supports open-source models, but given its relationship with OpenAI, and especially Anthropic's export controls, we doubt it.

WHY IT MATTERS
Three things are happening in this letter at once. First, there's the Youngbloods' "Get Together" vibe: the industry linking arms in open-ecosystem solidarity, ostensibly for AI and American prosperity. Second, there's the motive of heading off restrictions, preempting a government that wants more control and, sooner or later, will find its justification. Third, there's Nvidia's version: selective openness pitched, as any good businessman would pitch it, as good for the company. The irony shouldn't be lost. Huang runs the company that, by IDC's May 2026 estimate, controls roughly 81% of the data-center AI chip market, yet he's preaching an open ecosystem, as long as it's not in the sector he owns.
The other 24 signatories, companies like Microsoft, Meta, Dell, Palantir, IBM, and CrowdStrike to the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz and the accelerator Y Combinator, seem to believe they're stronger together than apart. Those six companies, plus Nvidia, are worth about $10.5 trillion combined or roughly 15% of the entire S&P 500. Nvidia alone is half of that, at ~$5 trillion. By making his feelings on open-weight models public for the first time, in his first-ever post on X, Jensen is signaling he'll go head-to-head with the federal government because he can.
"With great AI, open models, it's great for the whole industry…there will be more use. Whenever there will be more use, you'll have to sell more Nvidia computers, we'll have to build more data centers, we'll have more services, and the technology will diffuse into more industries," Huang said in an interview with Axios.
Open models increase demand for Nvidia's chips and make AI cheaper for businesses in the U.S. and around the world, with the biggest "losers" being frontier AI companies and the government trying to control the whole game.
WHAT'S NEXT
Nvidia forecasts $1 trillion in total sales for its Blackwell and Vera Rubin architectures across 2026 and 2027. That can't happen if the federal government suddenly restricts Jensen's customer base from using open-weight models, whether from Chinese labs or elsewhere.
As Huang said, "Great models lead to great use, which leads to great growth."
A market with only closed models, however great, could threaten usage. And less usage means less growth, ultimately hurting Nvidia's stock price.
